Convincing: patching opens >= 50% of the gap and steering shrinks the status length gap by >= 50% while the random control does < 15% and accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose. Indecision band: 20-50% effect, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% effect or a random control matching the real direction means the representation is correlational, refuting the causal mediation of H3 and the debiasing claim of H4.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 modulators and generalization): Tests where the status-effort gap is strongest and whether the probe/steering transfer without retraining. Data: reuses Experiment 1 problems and derived vectors. Factors: status-signal strength (explicit title vs subtle cue), first- vs third-person framing, and domain (clinical status on GPQA/medical items as highest-stakes). Transfer test: apply the 7B-derived probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting; compare RL-tuned vs distilled models for gap size. Systems compared: strong vs subtle status cues; in-model probe vs transferred probe; RL-tuned vs distilled. Decisive metric: change in the status length gap across each factor, first; plus transferred-probe Spearman relative to in-model. Convincing: at least one factor (expected: explicit clinical status on high-stakes items) yields a significantly larger gap than neutral phrasing, and the transferred probe retains >= 70% of in-model correlation. Indecision band: a transferred-probe correlation of 40-70% of in-model, or factor differences within noise, is reported as weak generalization. Negative result: no factor modulating the gap and transferred correlation < 40% means the effect is idiosyncratic and does not generalize, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The status effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences across personas rather than status per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, and the ladder design (varying status while matching wording style) isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. The effect may be small or absent in strongly instruction/safety-tuned models that are trained to treat all users equally (itself a valuable, publishable boundary condition). The status-effort signal may be inseparable from difficulty or from a generic sycophancy direction; the separability analysis, patching, and comparison to a difficulty/sycophancy probe address this, and overlap with a sycophancy direction would be an interesting mechanistic finding. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Persona framing may interact with content (e.g., clinical personas on medical items), which we treat as a modulator rather than a confound. Effects and their sign may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: length_prior_anchoring
Title: The Self-Fulfilling Length Prior: A Pre-Generation Budget Representation That Sets Reasoning Length Before Reasoning Begins
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models decide roughly how long to think before they think. The core, falsifiable claim is a causal dissociation: the prompt-final hidden state (before any reasoning token is emitted) linearly encodes an expected-length / budget prior that is shifted by a priori-specified SUPERFICIAL prompt features -- verbosity cues ('think carefully / be thorough' vs 'answer concisely'), elaborate vs terse phrasing, and number-format/surface presentation -- independently of the problem's true difficulty and correct answer, and this prior causally and self-fulfillingly sets trace length. These features should move budget rather than difficulty because they signal expected effort/register, not the problem's underlying computational demand. Steering the pre-generation prior changes trace length largely independently of accuracy, revealing that a chunk of overthinking (and some underthinking) is a mis-set, manipulable budget, not a reasoning need -- which also makes trace length a lever an adversary or a careless prompt can inflate.
Related Work: We contrast against the three closest lines and name the exact experiment each did not run. Difficulty-budgeting work reads a pre-generation signal to ALLOCATE compute (Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism; CODA/AdaCtrl budgeting) but assumes that signal tracks genuine difficulty and never holds the problem fixed while varying only surface form -- so it never tests whether the prior is difficulty-independent. Early-signal work reads correctness/commitment a few tokens IN (Temporal Predictors of Outcome; Chain-of-Probe) and 'Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning' shows the first step shapes outcomes -- but all read DURING generation and treat length as an emergent consequence, never a pre-token-boundary budget; none decode a length prior before a single reasoning token exists. Length-steering/editing work (ThinkEdit, Efficiency Steering, S3-CoT) can move realized length but studies a during-generation length direction, not a pre-committed prior nor its dissociation from difficulty. Our distinct, untested claim is that (a) a length/budget prior is set at the prompt boundary before any reasoning token, (b) it is dissociable from difficulty because it is partly driven by pre-specified superficial features, and (c) it causally, self-fulfillingly determines trace length. This is neither another difficulty-budgeting method nor an early-exit signal; it reframes a slice of miscalibrated compute allocation as an anchored, manipulable prior. It also differs from our prior proposals, which read DURING generation whether the answer is known and then stop; here the operative signal precedes generation and concerns budget, not answer-commitment.
Abstract: Reasoning language models produce chains of thought whose length varies enormously, and this length is usually assumed to reflect how much reasoning a problem actually requires. We challenge that assumption with a user-facing consequence in view: fewer tokens, lower latency and cost at the same accuracy, and defense against prompt-driven cost inflation. We hypothesize that models set an approximate length budget before they begin reasoning: the hidden state at the prompt boundary, prior to any reasoning token, linearly encodes an expected-length prior that is only partly tied to true difficulty and is also driven by pre-specified superficial features (verbosity cues like 'think carefully,' elaborate vs terse phrasing, number formatting, question framing). The model then generates to fill this budget, making it self-fulfilling. We test this on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA using open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). First, a linear probe on prompt-final activations predicts eventual trace length before any reasoning occurs, above a difficulty probe. Second, we run the decisive causal dissociation: holding the underlying problem fixed and varying only surface phrasing (human-verified to leave answer and difficulty intact), we show the length prior and realized length shift while accuracy does not, with pre-registered accuracy-invariance criteria and powered sample sizes. Third, we steer the length-prior direction and measure that trace length moves while accuracy stays flat, indicating mis-set budget. We localize the carrying components via activation patching. The framing serves two audiences: deployment cost control, and robustness against prompt manipulation that silently inflates compute -- via an interpretable, training-free length knob.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — A length/budget prior is linearly decodable at the prompt boundary before reasoning begins): Tests that the prompt-final hidden state predicts eventual trace length above and beyond difficulty. Data: GSM8K (1319 test), MATH500 (500), AIME 2022-2024 (90), GPQA-Diamond (198) — use all of the smaller sets and a 1000-problem sample of GSM8K; each problem produces one reasoning trace whose reasoning-token count is the label. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds (the length label is the median across seeds). Only linear probes are trained. Method: take the residual-stream activation at the last prompt token (before any reasoning token), and fit a ridge-regression probe per layer to predict trace length. Systems compared: the pre-generation probe vs two baselines that predict length from (i) prompt token-count and (ii) a pre-generation difficulty probe trained on empirical pass-rate. Decisive metric: Spearman correlation between predicted and realized length on held-out problems, and the partial correlation after regressing out the difficulty probe's prediction. Convincing result: Spearman >= 0.55 at some middle layer and a partial correlation >= 0.30 after removing difficulty — the prior carries length information beyond difficulty. Indecision band: partial correlation in [0.15, 0.30) means the prior is mostly (but not entirely) difficulty — reported as weak independent signal; below 0.15 means the pre-generation state adds nothing beyond difficulty and H1 fails. Negative result would mean length is not anchored pre-generation but emerges during reasoning, refuting the framing.

Experiment 2 (H2 — The prior is driven by superficial prompt features, not true difficulty): The core dissociation. Data: constructed — take 150 problems each from GSM8K, MATH500, and GPQA and generate 5 surface-variants per problem that hold the answer and true difficulty fixed while varying only phrasing (terse vs elaborate wording; appended 'think carefully and be thorough' vs 'answer concisely'; paraphrase; number-format change), giving 150x3x5 = 2250 variant prompts; human-check a 200-variant subset to confirm the answer and solution steps are unchanged. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) and 14B, frozen; the Experiment-1 probe reused. Systems compared: the same underlying problem across its surface variants. Decisive metric: the share of within-problem trace-length variance attributable to phrasing vs to residual difficulty, from a mixed-effects model with problem as a random effect. Secondary: whether the probe's predicted prior tracks the phrasing variant, and whether accuracy stays flat across variants. Convincing result: phrasing accounts for >= 30% of within-problem length variance while accuracy varies by < 3 points across variants and the probe prediction shifts with phrasing (Spearman >= 0.4 between predicted prior and variant verbosity). Indecision band: phrasing explaining [15%, 30%) of length variance is partial support — surface features matter but are secondary; below 15%, or accuracy itself shifting > 3 points across variants (variants changed difficulty), means the dissociation fails. Negative result (length invariant to phrasing at fixed difficulty) would mean the prior is difficulty-driven after all, an informative refutation of the 'superficial' claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Steering the prior causally and self-fulfillingly sets trace length, largely independent of accuracy): The causal test. Data: held-out 400 problems spanning GSM8K/MATH500/GPQA, not used to fit probes. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) and 14B (transfer), frozen; the only intervention is adding a length-prior direction to the prompt-final residual state before generation. The direction is the difference-of-means between short-trace and long-trace prompt-final activations; coefficient swept over a dose-response grid; 3 seeds. Systems compared: (i) no steering, (ii) positive steer (lengthen), (iii) negative steer (shorten), (iv) matched random-direction steer of equal norm, (v) difficulty-direction steer. Decisive metric: change in realized trace length as a function of steering dose, paired with accuracy change. Convincing result: a monotone dose-response in which negative steering cuts median length by >= 20% with accuracy change within +/- 1.5 points (in the overthinking regime), the effect exceeding the random-direction control by >= 10 points of length change, and positive steering lengthening traces — length moves specifically with the length-prior direction. Indecision band: an accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.5] points during shortening is the zone where the budget was partly needed — reported as a length-accuracy trade, not clean self-fulfillment; a length change indistinguishable (< 5%) from the random control means no causal prior. Negative result (length does not move, or moves only with accuracy loss > 3 points) would refute self-fulfillment.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Localization of the causal prior): Tests which components carry it. Data: 300 paired short-budget and long-budget prompts (from Experiment 2 variants with divergent realized length). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen. Method: activation patching of the prompt-final activation from a short-budget prompt into a long-budget prompt and vice versa, at candidate layers/components. Decisive metric: the shift in realized trace length attributable to each patched component. Convincing result: a small set of layers (<= 3) whose patching shifts median length by >= 20% and whose ablation reproduces the Experiment-3 steering effect. Indecision band: if no component shifts length by >= 10%, the prior is distributed — consistent with H1/H3 but not localizable, reported as such. Negative result would weaken the mechanistic account without touching the probe/steering evidence.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Mis-set budget is a slice of overthinking and underthinking, and re-setting the prior saves tokens at equal accuracy): Tests the efficiency payoff. Data: held-out 400 problems with a per-problem 'needed length' estimated by truncate-and-resume (the minimal prefix after which the correct answer is recoverable). Model: 7B and 14B, frozen; training-free correction = steer the prior toward the difficulty-appropriate target length. Systems compared: (i) no intervention, (ii) prior-correction steering, (iii) fixed truncation, (iv) budget-forcing prompt baseline. Decisive metric: tokens-at-fixed-accuracy (median token reduction subject to accuracy not dropping beyond the noise band), reported separately for prior-overshoot (overthinking) and prior-undershoot (underthinking) problems. Secondary: fraction of problems whose prior is mis-set relative to needed length; wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: prior-correction cuts median tokens by >= 15% at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, beating fixed truncation at matched accuracy, and recovers accuracy on >= 10% of underthinking items by lengthening them. Indecision band: token reduction in [5%, 15%) or accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.0] points is a weak/traded outcome, reported as such. Negative result (no net token saving at fixed accuracy) would bound the practical value while leaving the mechanistic claims (H1-H3) intact.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 — Generalization across datasets and scales): Tests transfer without refitting. Data: the four datasets and the four model sizes above. Method: apply the probe and steering direction fit on one dataset/model to the others without retraining. Decisive metric: retained length-prediction Spearman and retained steering length-change effect on the transfer targets. Convincing result: >= two-thirds of in-domain probe correlation and steering effect retained across datasets, and a monotone (if attenuated) effect across scales. Indecision band: retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means partial, calibration-dependent transfer; below one-third means the prior is model/dataset-specific. Negative result would confine the phenomenon to the fitting conditions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The pre-generation length prior may be strongly correlated with genuine difficulty, making the dissociation hard to establish; the fixed-problem surface-variant design directly targets this, and a null dissociation would itself be an informative result (length is difficulty-driven after all). Surface-variant construction could inadvertently change difficulty; we mitigate by verifying answer/accuracy invariance and using human-checked paraphrases. Steering the prior may push activations off-distribution and degrade coherence, confounding the accuracy read; we report sample validity and use matched-direction controls. Reducing a mis-set long budget may still hurt accuracy on some items (the budget was partly needed), bounding the efficiency claim; the truncate-and-resume needed-length analysis characterizes this. Trace-length regression is noisy for short traces; we focus on tasks with substantial reasoning. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and the strength of surface-feature influence likely varies with instruction tuning.

Name: tokenizer_fragmentation_overthinking
Title: Fragmented Numbers, Longer Thoughts: How Tokenizer Segmentation of Numerals Inflates Reasoning Compute Independent of Difficulty
Short Hypothesis: For the identical math problem, a reasoning model spends systematically more thinking tokens when the numbers are tokenized into more fragments (worse digit segmentation), and this excess is not extra genuine reasoning but a surface-form artifact: the tokenizer's fragmentation inflates an internal difficulty/length signal read before reasoning begins. Re-encoding the same numbers into fewer, cleaner tokens (e.g., digit-spacing or single-digit segmentation) reduces reasoning length at equal accuracy. We pre-register the estimand as the effect of fragments-per-number on thinking length after controlling for raw prompt token count and problem identity, and we test whether it is mediated by a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation that activation patching between matched prompts can causally move.
Related Work: Numeral-system work (Scaling Behavior regarding Numeral Systems, 2024) shows base-10/1-digit tokenization is more data-efficient for TRAINING and studies accuracy, not inference-time compute. Benford's Curse (2025) traces digit-generation bias to pretraining statistics and later-layer FFN neurons, focused on hallucination/accuracy, not reasoning length. 'Say Anything but This' (2026) shows tokenizer non-uniqueness causes reasoning failures (phantom edits) but again targets correctness, not compute allocation. Cognitive-arithmetic psychology (Yip 2006/2010) shows humans take longer to verify equations in word vs digit surface form and with larger problem size, motivating a human-to-LLM transfer. Efficient-reasoning interpretability (FR-Ponder 2025, difficulty-perception probes) reads a scalar difficulty/length signal to allocate compute but treats that signal as tracking genuine difficulty and never asks whether it is contaminated by tokenizer segmentation. No prior work (a) measures a reasoning-COMPUTE (token) gap driven by numeral tokenization on matched problems, (b) dissociates it from true difficulty, or (c) locates and causally tests a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation. This unites tokenizer/interpretability and efficient-reasoning literatures around an inference-time compute-allocation artifact, and is distinct from all prior proposals (none touch tokenizer/surface form).
Abstract: Reasoning language models allocate a thinking budget assumed to reflect a problem's genuine difficulty. We ask whether this budget is partly contaminated by a superficial factor: how the tokenizer segments the numbers in the prompt. Modern subword tokenizers split numerals inconsistently ('1234' as one, two, or four tokens depending on context and format), and we hypothesize that more fragmented numerals lead a reasoning model to think longer on the exact same problem, inflating tokens without improving accuracy. Because digit-spacing also lengthens the prompt, we separate three factors -- mathematical content, raw prompt token count, and numeral segmentation -- and pre-register the estimand as the effect of fragments-per-number on thinking length after controlling for prompt length and problem identity, including a length-matched synthetic-numeral control. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and arithmetic-heavy word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we build format variants of identical problems that hold content and answer fixed while varying only numeral tokenization (native BPE, digit-spaced, comma-grouped, single-digit), tokenizer-verified to change fragment counts, and we check that accuracy and solution-path quality are unchanged. Mechanistically, we test whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a fragmentation-sensitive length signal separable from a true-difficulty signal, and probe its causal role via activation patching between matched prompts, difference-of-means steering, and random-direction and unrelated-length-signal controls. If it holds, re-encoding numbers into fewer tokens is a training-free fix that could cut thinking tokens by roughly 15% at fixed accuracy -- relevant to inference-optimization, tokenizer-design, efficient-reasoning, and interpretability audiences, and arguing for controlling numeral surface form when benchmarking reasoning models.
Experiments:
All runs use open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). All model weights are frozen throughout; the only trainable objects are small linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors described below. Decoding is fixed at temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, with 5 sampled traces per (problem, format) using seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count over the 5 seeds and accuracy is the mean exact-match over them. Reasoning tokens are counted between the think-open and think-close delimiters. Compute fits one 80GB GPU; the 14B model uses the largest budget and is run only on the reduced subset noted in each experiment.

Experiment 1 (H1 - fragmentation inflates thinking length on identical problems): Tests whether, for a fixed math problem, more fragmented numeral tokenization yields more thinking tokens. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319 items) and MATH500 (500 items); we sample 400 GSM8K and 200 MATH500 problems that contain at least one multi-digit number (stratified by number magnitude), because per-problem 4-format x 5-seed x 4-model generation is the cost driver and 600 problems already give within-problem paired power. For each seed problem we build four content-identical format variants that change only numeral segmentation: (a) native BPE, (b) digit-spaced ('1 2 3 4'), (c) comma/underscore-grouped ('1,234'), (d) forced single-digit. We verify with each model's own tokenizer that fragments-per-number differ across variants and that the decoded prompt and gold answer are otherwise identical. We additionally include a length-matched synthetic-numeral control in which high- and low-fragmentation variants are padded to identical total prompt token counts, isolating segmentation from raw length, and we verify that solution-path quality (correctness of intermediate arithmetic steps, not just the final answer) is unchanged across variants on a step-checked subsample. Systems compared: the four format variants of the same problem, within model. Decisive metric: within-problem paired difference in mean thinking tokens between the highest- and lowest-fragmentation variant, as a median relative increase across problems. Convincing: median relative increase >= 15% with a paired Wilcoxon test (Holm-corrected across models) and accuracy differences within +/-1 point across variants. Indecision band: a median relative increase between 5% and 15% is treated as not deciding H1 - reported as a weak/again-inconclusive effect that does not license the mechanism experiments. Negative result: below 5%, or accuracy moving with format, means numeral fragmentation does not inflate reasoning length and H1 is rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the excess is a surface-form artifact, not genuine reasoning): Tests whether fragmentation adds wasted tokens rather than needed reasoning, and whether the length gap survives after removing intrinsic problem difficulty and raw prompt length. Data: the same 600 problems and four variants from Experiment 1 (reusing the generated traces; no new problems). Analysis 1 (dissociation): fit a mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per problem identity (absorbing intrinsic difficulty) and fixed effects for fragments-per-number and for raw prompt token count (a covariate, since digit-spacing lengthens the prompt); we also compare the single-digit vs comma-grouped contrast, which moves fragmentation while holding or reversing prompt length. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine): using truncate-and-resume, estimate the minimal-solve length per variant (shortest prefix that still yields the correct answer on resume) on a 150-problem subsample (cost of resume sweeps), and test whether fragmentation raises the gap between actual and minimal-solve length rather than the minimal-solve length itself; additionally tag the extra tokens by whether they re-read/restate the numbers (string-match on the numerals). Systems compared: fragmentation effect with vs without the difficulty random effect and the prompt-length covariate. We also include a heuristic baseline that predicts thinking length from prompt token count alone and require fragments-per-number to add predictive power beyond it. Decisive metric: the standardized fixed-effect coefficient of fragments-per-number on thinking length after both controls, first; supported by the fraction of fragmentation-induced extra tokens falling in the wasted (beyond-minimal) portion. Convincing: the fragmentation coefficient stays significant (95% CI excluding 0) with at least half of its length effect surviving the prompt-length covariate, and >= 60% of the extra tokens landing in the wasted portion. Indecision band: if 30-60% of extra tokens are wasted, or the surviving coefficient is significant but under half the raw effect, the artifact framing is only partially supported and reported as such. Negative result: the fragmentation coefficient vanishing under controls, or extra tokens being predominantly genuine (<30% wasted), means the length gap reflects real added parsing difficulty rather than an artifact, refuting H2's 'not genuine reasoning' claim.

Experiment 3 (H4 - a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation exists and is separable from true difficulty): Tests whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a length signal that rises with fragmentation and is distinguishable from a genuine-difficulty signal. Data: activations at the final prompt token (before the first thinking token) for the 600 problems x 4 variants from Experiment 1, split 70/15/15 into train/val/test by problem identity so no problem crosses splits. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) with a layer sweep; probes are ridge-regression linear readouts (L2 chosen on val). We train a fragmentation-length probe (target = observed thinking length) and, for comparison, a true-difficulty probe (target = per-problem pass-rate over seeds). Systems compared: for identical-content problem pairs differing only in fragmentation, does the length probe's prediction increase with fragment count; and how aligned are the length-direction and difficulty-direction (principal angle) and their joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: held-out Spearman correlation between the length probe's prediction and fragments-per-number on matched problems, first; plus the principal angle between the two probe directions. Convincing: Spearman >= 0.3 (p<0.01) at the best layer, principal angle >= 30 degrees (directions not collinear), and the length probe adding significant R2 over the difficulty probe in a joint model. Indecision band: Spearman 0.15-0.3, or principal angle 20-30 degrees, is treated as a present-but-entangled signal that does not by itself confirm a separable representation. Negative result: Spearman < 0.15 or angle < 20 degrees means either no readable fragmentation signal or one indistinguishable from difficulty, weakening the separability part of H4.

Experiment 4 (H4 - the length-budget representation causally mediates the inflation): Tests whether editing the boundary representation moves reasoning length as predicted. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1) each with a matched low- and high-fragmentation variant; frozen 7B model (with a 1.5B replication). Intervention A (activation patching): patch the boundary residual state from the low-fragmentation variant into the matched high-fragmentation forward pass at the layer localized in Experiment 3, and measure the change in thinking length. Intervention B (difference-of-means steering, training-free fix): derive a steering direction from low-minus-high fragmentation boundary states on the Experiment 3 train split, add it (dose swept over 4 magnitudes) to high-fragmentation prompts at inference. Controls: a matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm, and an off-target accuracy check on held-out problems. Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random-direction control vs no intervention. Decisive metric: reduction in thinking tokens on high-fragmentation prompts toward the low-fragmentation level, first, reported as the fraction of the fragmentation gap closed; with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: real patch/steer closes >= 50% of the fragmentation length gap while the random-direction control closes < 15% and accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose. Indecision band: closing 20-50% of the gap, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is treated as partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% of the gap closed, or the random control matching the real direction, means the representation is correlational not causal, refuting the causal-mediation claim of H4.

Experiment 5 (H3 - re-encoding into fewer tokens reduces reasoning length at equal accuracy): Tests the deployable input-side fix and its practical payoff. Data: the full GSM8K test (1319) and MATH500 (500), each rendered in native BPE vs a low-fragmentation re-encoding (digit-grouping numbers into as few tokens as the tokenizer allows), tokenizer-verified to reduce fragments-per-number and to preserve the gold answer; run on 1.5B, 7B, and 14B (14B on a 300-problem subsample for budget). Systems compared: native encoding, low-fragmentation re-encoding, and the Experiment-4 steering fix, plus a fixed-truncation baseline at matched mean length. Decisive metric: mean thinking tokens at matched accuracy (accuracy within +/-1 point of native), first; secondary wall-clock speedup. Convincing: the re-encoding cuts mean thinking tokens by >= 15% with accuracy within +/-1 point, on at least the 7B and 14B models, and the effect grows for models with coarser native numeral tokenization. Indecision band: a 5-15% token reduction, or accuracy slipping 1-2 points, is a marginal win reported without strong claims. Negative result: < 5% reduction or an accuracy drop > 2 points means re-encoding is not a free efficiency win, refuting H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The fragmentation effect could be an artifact of prompt token-length (digit-spacing lengthens the prompt) rather than segmentation per se; the prompt-length covariate, length-matched format comparisons, and the single-digit-vs-grouped contrast (which vary fragmentation at similar or opposite prompt lengths) are designed to isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Number re-formatting could inadvertently change accuracy or difficulty; we verify answer/accuracy invariance and use tokenizer-verified content-identical variants. The fragmentation-length signal may be inseparable from a true-difficulty signal if the model genuinely finds fragmented numbers harder to parse (which would still be a novel, actionable phenomenon but weaken the 'artifact' framing); the separability analysis and patching address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound the accuracy read; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Effects likely depend on the model's numeral-tokenization scheme and may be small for models already using clean single-digit tokenization (itself an informative boundary condition). Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters, limiting to models with explicit thinking segments; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

Name: tokenizer_fragmentation_overthinking
Title: Fragmented Numbers, Longer Thoughts: A Tokenizer-Induced Compute Tax in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: We make two separable claims about numeral tokenization and reasoning compute. CLAIM 1 (phenomenon): for the identical math problem, a reasoning model spends systematically more thinking tokens when its numbers are tokenized into more fragments (worse digit segmentation) at EQUAL accuracy — the novelty is compute inflation at matched accuracy, not the already-known result that fragmentation hurts arithmetic correctness. CLAIM 2 (mechanism): this inflation is partially mediated by a fragmentation-sensitive length/difficulty signal read at the prompt boundary BEFORE reasoning begins — a learned budget predictor, distinct from a broad post-hoc length prior — which would be falsified if the prompt-boundary probe shows no fragmentation-driven shift for identical problems or the shift does not correlate with token inflation. Re-encoding the same numbers into fewer, cleaner tokens (a deployable, training-free input-side fix) reduces reasoning length at equal accuracy, and activation patching tests whether the fragmentation-sensitive representation is causally involved. The practical payoff is cheaper inference with no retraining: on numeral-heavy reasoning streams, input-side digit grouping recovers wasted tokens, cutting latency and serving cost — relevant to evaluation harnesses, inference serving, tokenizer design, and reasoning distillation. We scope the reach to numeral-heavy reasoning, not all natural-language tasks, and note models already using clean single-digit tokenization may show no effect.
Related Work: We separate two prior families and give each a one-line delta. (1) Overthinking / verbosity control (Efficiency Steering, CREST, Manifold Steering, ReflCtrl, STU-PID, NEAT early-exit; The First Impression Problem) treats the pre-generation length/difficulty signal as tracking GENUINE difficulty and studies a fixed textual form; our delta is that a purely SURFACE tokenization change inflates that budget on content-identical problems. (2) Numeral tokenization (Scaling Behavior of Numeral Systems; Benford's Curse; Say Anything but This on tokenizer non-uniqueness) studies training efficiency, accuracy, and hallucination, not inference-time COMPUTE; our delta is a reasoning-compute tax at matched accuracy, dissociated from true parsing difficulty, with a localized prompt-boundary budget signal. No prior work measures a reasoning-compute gap driven by numeral tokenization on matched problems, dissociates it from genuine difficulty via a numerals-only parsing control, or causally tests a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation — the union of the tokenizer and efficient-reasoning literatures that we contribute.
Abstract: Reasoning language models allocate a thinking budget assumed to reflect a problem's genuine difficulty. We show this budget is contaminated by a superficial factor: how the tokenizer segments the numbers in the prompt. Modern subword tokenizers split numerals inconsistently ('1234' as one, two, or four tokens depending on format), and we hypothesize that more fragmented numerals cause a model to think longer on the exact same problem, inflating tokens without improving accuracy. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and arithmetic-heavy word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we construct content-identical variants that hold the mathematical content and answer fixed while varying only numeral tokenization (native BPE, digit-spaced, comma-grouped, single-digit segmentation), verified via the tokenizer to change fragment counts. We measure reasoning-token count and accuracy per variant and test whether fragmentation predicts thinking length independent of difficulty via a mixed-effects decomposition, controlling for raw prompt length. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a fragmentation-sensitive length/difficulty signal dissociable from a true-difficulty probe, localize it, causally validate via activation patching (patch a low-fragmentation state into a high-fragmentation context and observe the budget drop), and steer it to cancel the inflation. We report phenomenon and mechanism as two separately falsifiable claims and translate the effect into deployment terms: the recoverable share of reasoning tokens on a numeral-heavy stream and the corresponding latency and serving-cost reduction achievable with no retraining. Our work reveals a tokenizer-induced overthinking artifact, offers a simple training-free fix (re-encoding numbers) plus a mechanistic account localized to a prompt-boundary budget signal, and scopes its reach to numeral-heavy reasoning — relevant to evaluation harnesses, inference serving, tokenizer design, and reasoning distillation.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B thinking mode); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Seed problems come from existing sets used as-is: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), and arithmetic-heavy word problems (300 items). For each seed we CONSTRUCT content-identical variants that change ONLY numeral tokenization — (a) native BPE, (b) digit-spaced ('1 2 3 4'), (c) comma/underscore-grouped ('1,234'), (d) single-digit forced segmentation — and confirm via the model's own tokenizer that fragment counts differ while decoded meaning and the correct answer are identical. Compute forces subsampling of the trace-heavy conditions to 400 GSM8K, 400 MATH500, and all 300 word problems, each in all four encodings, 3 seeds.

Experiment 1 (H1 — fragmentation inflates thinking length): Tests whether higher numeral fragmentation increases reasoning tokens on the same problem at equal accuracy. Data: the four encodings above. Decisive metric FIRST: within-problem reasoning-token count as a function of numeral fragment count, at matched accuracy. Convincing result: reasoning tokens rise monotonically with fragment count by >= 15% median from the least- to most-fragmented encoding while accuracy stays within 1 point, in >=3 of 4 models on >=2 of 3 sources. Indecision band: token inflation 5-15% — a modest tax, reported as limited. Negative result (no inflation, or accuracy changes so it is not equal-accuracy): tokenizer fragmentation does not inflate compute; H1 fails and the mechanistic experiments are not pursued.

Experiment 2 (H1 — segmentation, not prompt length): Tests that the effect is fragment count, not raw prompt length. Data: Experiment-1 variants, exploiting that single-digit vs grouped encodings vary fragmentation at similar or opposite prompt lengths. Analysis: mixed-effects model of reasoning length with random effect for problem identity and fixed effects for fragment count and raw prompt length. Decisive metric FIRST: the fragment-count fixed effect after absorbing problem identity and prompt length. Convincing result: fragment-count effect survives (CI excluding 0) with problem identity and prompt length absorbed, and holds in length-matched format contrasts. Indecision band: fragment-count effect present but its length-matched contrast CI overlaps 0 — possibly length-driven. Negative result (effect vanishes after length control): the phenomenon is a prompt-length artifact, an informative null; H1's segmentation claim fails.

Experiment 3 (H1 — wasted, not genuine reasoning): Tests that the extra tokens are wasted, not genuine number-parsing reasoning. Data: 200 items/source with truncate-and-resume minimal-solve length per variant (minimal-solve = shortest resume-from-boundary continuation that still reaches the correct answer, averaged over resume points), lexical tagging of number re-reading/restatement, and a decisive true-parsing control — a numerals-only recognition/parsing task carrying the SAME token fragments but NO arithmetic, whose latency/accuracy isolates genuine parsing cost from reasoning inflation. Decisive metric FIRST: the increase in WASTED tokens (beyond minimal solve) with fragment count, and rate of number re-reading. Convincing result: fragmentation inflates wasted tokens and number-restatement (CI excluding 0) while minimal-solve length is unchanged. Indecision band: minimal-solve length itself rises 5-15% with fragmentation — fragmented numbers are genuinely a bit harder to parse, weakening the 'artifact' framing (reported as such). Negative result (minimal-solve rises as much as total): the extra compute is genuine parsing difficulty, not a surface artifact; the 'artifact' claim fails though the phenomenon stands.

Experiment 4 (H2 — fragmentation-sensitive length signal at the prompt boundary): Tests that the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a length signal that rises with fragmentation for identical problems, dissociable from true difficulty. Data: prompt-boundary (last prompt token, pre-reasoning) activations from Experiment-1 variants; a length-predicting probe (ridge) and a true-difficulty probe (trained on pass-rate) per layer, item-level 70/15/15 split, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Decisive metric FIRST: the shift in the length-probe prediction for identical problems between low- and high-fragmentation encodings, and the principal angle between the fragmentation-length direction and the true-difficulty direction. Convincing result: the length-probe prediction rises monotonically with fragment count for identical problems (CI excluding 0), correlates with Experiment-1 token inflation, and the fragmentation-length direction is separable from true difficulty (angle >= 30 degrees). Indecision band: probe shift present but correlation with token inflation |r| < 0.3, or angle 15-30 degrees — weakly evidenced/entangled. Negative result (no probe shift for identical problems): no fragmentation-sensitive length representation; H2 fails.

Experiment 5 (H4 — causal mediation by patching): Tests that the fragmentation-sensitive representation causally drives the extra compute. Data: 300 problems in both low- and high-fragmentation encodings. Intervention: activation-patch the prompt-boundary state from the low-fragmentation variant into the matched high-fragmentation context (same problem) at localized components; frozen weights; dose-response; reverse patch for bidirectionality. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) low-fragmentation patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in reasoning length toward the low-fragmentation level under the patch versus controls, accuracy preserved. Convincing result: the low-fragmentation patch removes >= half the fragmentation-driven inflation with CI excluding 0, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy within 1 point; reverse patch inflates length. Indecision band: removal 20-50% of the inflation, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of it — causality not clean. Negative result (no reduction, or non-specific): the representation is not causal; H4 fails.

Experiment 6 (H3 — re-encoding fix and debiasing steer): Tests that reducing fragmentation cuts reasoning length at equal accuracy. Data: full evaluation sets, 3 seeds, high-fragmentation native inputs. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) input-side re-encoding of numbers into fewer tokens (deployable preprocessing fix), (c) fragmentation-length debiasing steer (difference-of-means between low- and high-fragmentation boundary states, applied at problem onset), (d) fixed truncation. Decisive metric FIRST: tokens-at-equal-accuracy relative to the native-fragmentation baseline. Convincing result: both the re-encoding fix and the steer cut tokens by >= 15% at accuracy within 1 point of native. Indecision band: token savings 5-15%, or a 1-3 point accuracy cost — a modest gain, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no token savings at equal accuracy): neither fix delivers the benefit; H3 fails though H1-H2 stand.

Experiment 7 (practical payoff and generalization): Tests the deployment payoff and transfer. Data: a mixed problem stream, and probe/steer fit on one set+model applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B. Decisive metric FIRST: total tokens wasted on the stream by native fragmentation versus an oracle low-fragmentation encoding, and cross-set transfer of the fix. Convincing result: native fragmentation wastes >= 10% of stream reasoning tokens recoverable by input-side digit grouping, transfer retains >= half the in-domain savings, and the effect is stronger for models with coarser numeral tokenization. Indecision band: recoverable waste 3-10%, or transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain — a small but real win. Negative result (no recoverable waste, no transfer): the effect is negligible or idiosyncratic per model, reported as a boundary characterization (models already using clean single-digit tokenization may show no effect).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The fragmentation effect could be an artifact of prompt token-length (digit-spacing lengthens prompts) rather than segmentation per se; the length covariate, length-matched comparisons, and single-digit-vs-grouped contrasts isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Number re-formatting could inadvertently change accuracy/difficulty; we verify answer/accuracy invariance and use tokenizer-verified content-identical variants. The fragmentation-length signal may be inseparable from a true-difficulty signal if the model genuinely finds fragmented numbers harder to parse (still a novel, actionable phenomenon but weakening the 'artifact' framing); the separability analysis and patching address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Effects likely depend on the model's numeral-tokenization scheme and may be small for models already using clean single-digit tokenization (an informative boundary condition). Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

Name: difficulty_contraction_failure
Title: Difficulty That Won't Shrink: Overthinking as a Failure of the Internal Difficulty Signal to Contract as Reasoning Progresses
Short Hypothesis: LLMs carry a linearly-decodable, attention-head-mediated 'difficulty' representation that prior work reads only once, before generation. We hypothesize this signal should contract during a chain of thought as sub-goals are resolved, and that overthinking occurs when this contraction fails - the internal difficulty stays high even after residual work reaches zero. Concretely: reading the SAME final-layer difficulty heads and difficulty direction at step boundaries, decoded difficulty should decline monotonically with truncate-and-resume residual work on well-behaved traces, and overthought traces are those where it plateaus high despite zero residual work; steering those heads toward the easy pole once residual work is low should induce early, correct termination, and this effect must remain after matching on a confidence/uncertainty probe.
Related Work: A recent cluster of interpretability work establishes that LLMs linearly encode problem difficulty in pre-generation activations, localize it to specific final-layer attention heads (Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism, 2025; A Shared Geometry of Difficulty, 2026; LLMs Encode Their Failures, 2026), and use it to allocate compute at the input level (ACTSC 2026, FR-Ponder 2025, AdaCtrl 2025, CODA 2026, UAB 2026). All treat difficulty as a static, pre-generation property of the input and set a budget or sample count before or independent of the trace; none examine how the difficulty representation evolves DURING generation or connect overthinking to a failure of that representation to update. Our contribution is orthogonal and temporally specific: (1) the same difficulty direction/heads can be read at intermediate CoT positions and normally contract as work is completed; (2) overthinking is a specific dynamical failure - non-contracting difficulty despite resolved residual work; (3) we intervene on the difficulty heads mid-generation to induce contraction. Critically, we separate this from confidence/uncertainty dynamics: confidence early-exit acts on a correctness/uncertainty readout, whereas we act on the difficulty heads and require the causal effect to survive matching on a confidence probe, so the claim is about difficulty specifically, not a generic confidence correlate.
Abstract: Deployed reasoning models waste large amounts of compute by continuing to reason after a problem is effectively solved, inflating tokens, latency, and serving cost with unreliable stopping. Recent interpretability work shows that LLMs linearly encode problem difficulty via specific attention heads and that this signal, read before generation, can allocate compute. But difficulty is not static: as a model resolves sub-goals, the residual problem becomes easier and its internal difficulty should shrink. We hypothesize that overthinking is a failure of this contraction - the internal difficulty stays elevated even after residual work reaches zero, driving continued reasoning. We replicate a linear difficulty probe and localize difficulty-sensitive final-layer heads on DeepSeek-R1 distills (1.5B-14B) and Qwen3, then read the signal at each step of a chain of thought on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA. We test whether difficulty normally contracts as residual work (truncate-and-resume) decreases, whether overthought traces show stalled difficulty, and whether the contraction-failure metric predicts wasted tokens better than absolute difficulty, length, or a confidence probe. We causally validate the difficulty heads by steering them toward the easy pole mid-generation once residual work is low - including a negative control that steers them when residual work is NOT low - and require the effect to persist after matching a confidence probe, isolating difficulty from confidence. We compare token savings, wall-clock latency, and per-query cost at equal accuracy against input-level difficulty budgeting, length steering, and confidence early-exit, and analyze failures where genuine difficulty persists. The work reframes a static difficulty representation as a dynamical control signal for interpretability, decoding, and agentic-inference practitioners.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trainable, and interventions are activation edits (no weight updates). Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198); difficulty labels from Easy2Hard-AMC-style annotations plus empirical per-item pass-rates (32 samples/item). All thresholds (contraction cutoff, residual-work threshold, k) are FIXED on a training split before any evaluation, to avoid post-hoc success criteria. Residual work is defined precisely as: truncate the trace at step t, force termination, read the forced answer; residual work at t = the minimum number of additional true steps (from the full trace) after which forced-exit accuracy first reaches and holds the final accuracy - reported alongside a simpler proxy (forced-exit correctness at t) for robustness.

Experiment 1 (H1 - Difficulty is decodable and head-mediated, including mid-trace): Replicate a linear difficulty probe and localize difficulty-sensitive final-layer heads, then test readability at intermediate positions. Train on pre-generation activations (40% of items), evaluate on 60% held out. Identify difficulty heads by ablation impact on probe output; report which layer/head set. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC/R^2 pre-generation and at intermediate positions. Convincing: pre-generation AUROC >= 0.75 (replication) and intermediate AUROC >= 0.70, with a small head set (<= 10) whose ablation drops probe AUROC by >= 0.1. Indecision: intermediate AUROC in [0.6, 0.7]. Negative (< 0.6): difficulty is encoded only pre-generation - this is the MINIMUM FALSIFIER: the paper then becomes a strong negative result (difficulty is not trackable during reasoning) and the novelty shifts to that finding.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Difficulty normally contracts): Form the step-wise difficulty trajectory over boundaries. Decisive metric: mean signed change in decoded difficulty from first to last step across correctly solved traces. Convincing: contracts on average (paired p < 0.01, mean drop > 0.3 in normalized probe units) on the majority of correctly solved traces. Indecision: mean drop in [0.1, 0.3]. Negative (< 0.1 or increasing): difficulty does not contract, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Contraction failure tracks residual work and predicts waste): Contraction failure = area between difficulty and residual-work trajectories after residual work hits zero (steps subsampled every 2nd boundary). First test difficulty-vs-residual-work correlation, then whether contraction failure predicts wasted tokens. Decisive metric: out-of-sample 5-fold R^2 of contraction failure predicting wasted tokens, minus best competitor among absolute pre-generation difficulty, trace length, and a confidence probe. Convincing: correlation r > 0.4 and contraction failure beats the best competitor by >= 0.10 R^2 on at least three datasets. Indecision: r in [0.2, 0.4] or R^2 advantage in [0.02, 0.10]. Negative (r < 0.2 or advantage <= 0.02): overthinking is not this pattern.

Experiment 4 (H4 - Difficulty heads causally gate continuation, isolated from confidence): At low-residual-work / high-difficulty boundaries, steer the localized difficulty heads toward the easy pole (or add the negative difficulty direction) and measure the effect on termination-token probability and continuation length, vs. (i) control heads, (ii) norm-matched random directions, and (iii) confidence-probe steering matched in magnitude. Ablations over head choice, layer choice, and intervention timing establish specificity. Decisive metric: increase in termination probability under difficulty-head steering minus that under control-head AND under confidence-probe steering. Convincing: difficulty-head steering raises termination probability by >= 15 points and shortens continuation by >= 20%, significantly above control/random AND above confidence-probe steering, with accuracy on already-solved items within 2 points. Indecision: gain in [5, 15] points over control. Negative (< 5 points over control, or indistinguishable from confidence-probe steering): difficulty heads are not a distinct causal gate.

Experiment 5 (H4 - Negative control on timing regime): Apply the same difficulty-head steering when residual work is NOT low (early, genuinely-hard boundaries) and confirm it does NOT induce correct early termination there. Decisive metric: termination-probability increase under steering in the low-residual-work regime minus that in the high-residual-work regime. Convincing: the termination effect is concentrated in the low-residual-work regime (difference >= 10 points), and steering in the high-residual-work regime harms accuracy (confirming it should not fire). Indecision: a weak regime difference. Negative (effect equal across regimes): early termination is not specific to the intended regime, weakening the mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H4 - Training-free intervention: savings, latency, cost): Online, read step-wise difficulty; when difficulty fails to contract but a residual-work probe (trained on Experiment-3 labels, 40/60 split) predicts low residual work for k consecutive steps, steer difficulty heads toward easy. k and threshold fixed on the training split. Report the full accuracy-vs-token Pareto curve. Systems compared on all four datasets: intervention vs. (a) no intervention, (b) fixed truncation matched to intervention budget, (c) input-level difficulty budgeting (CODA/AdaCtrl-style), (d) length steering, (e) confidence-based early-exit. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy. Secondary: mean tokens, accuracy, wall-clock latency, per-query serving cost. Convincing: >= 25% token reduction within 1 point on GSM8K and MATH500, on or above every baseline frontier. Indecision: reduction in [10%, 25%] or a frontier-tie - the dynamical characterization (Experiments 1-5) is then the standalone contribution. Negative (< 10% or > 1 point loss): no usable savings.

Experiment 7 (H4 - Underthinking guard): On the hardest quartile where residual work truly stays large, verify the trigger does not fire and does not induce premature termination. Decisive metric: hard-item accuracy drop vs. residual-work threshold. Convincing: < 1 point at the deployed threshold. Indecision: 1-3 point drop. Negative (> 3 point drop): the gate cannot protect hard items, bounding H4.

Experiment 8 (H1/H3 - Generality across data and scale): Transfer probe, head set, and trigger across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain and intervention token-savings retention. Convincing: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales; savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision: retention in [60%, 80%]. Negative (< 60%): the difficulty-dynamics signal is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The difficulty direction may entangle with confidence/uncertainty, blurring the distinction from confidence early-exit; we control by comparing difficulty-head steering against magnitude-matched confidence-probe steering and require the difficulty heads to be causally distinct. Difficulty may not be cleanly readable at intermediate positions (the probe was trained pre-generation); if it is only encoded pre-generation the dynamical framing collapses into a strong negative result (the stated minimum falsifier). The truncate-and-resume residual-work measure is noisy and compute-heavy; we subsample steps and report a simpler proxy. Steering difficulty heads could disrupt genuine hard-problem reasoning (underthinking); the residual-work-gated trigger, negative-control regime test, and threshold analysis address this. Intervention gains may not exceed strong difficulty-budgeting baselines; the standalone contribution is then the dynamical, causal characterization, useful to interpretability, decoding/efficiency, and agentic-inference communities that need reliable in-flight stopping. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

Name: dimensional_consistency_blindspot
Title: Right Number, Wrong Unit: An Internal Dimension Representation That Reasoning Models Encode But Fail to Consult
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models linearly encode the physical DIMENSION/unit-type of the current working quantity (length vs time vs mass vs concentration) in the residual stream at specific mid-to-late layers and step boundaries, separately from its numerical magnitude, but frequently fail to CONSULT this representation at the moment a dimensionally-inconsistent operation is committed (adding incompatible units, dropping a conversion, reporting the wrong unit). We split this into two independently falsifiable claims. REPRESENTATIONAL EXISTENCE: a probe decodes unit-type well above magnitude, task-format, and unit-token baselines, and survives lexical controls (synonyms, non-adjacent unit tokens) — i.e. it is an abstract dimension code, not a read of the literal 'mg' string. CONSULTATION GAP: on steps where the model commits a dimensional error, the operand unit-types are nonetheless decodable, so the information was available but unused (a know-but-dont-check gap), which activation patching shows to be causally involved in the error. Because dimension tracking is a reusable internal consistency check across physics, engineering, and quantitative science — not only medicine — a training-free dimensional-consistency monitor that reads the internal unit-type and flags incompatible operations could serve calculator-augmented reasoning, tool-use agents, and medical-NLP pipelines. We evaluate it on medication-STYLE dosing scenarios for their high stakes, without claiming clinical validation.
Related Work: We position against three threads and state the delta. (1) Numerical MAGNITUDE representations: work showing LLMs linearly encode log-magnitude and a mental-number-line (LLMs Know More About Numbers than They Can Say 2026; Number Representations as Human Mental Number Line 2025) and that irrelevant numbers perturb them (Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding 2025; Probing for Arithmetic Errors 2025); all concern HOW BIG a number is and arithmetic correctness — never the physical DIMENSION/unit-TYPE of a quantity, which is our target representation and which we show is separable from magnitude. (2) NUMCoT and numeric-reasoning benchmarks quantify unit/conversion error RATES behaviorally but neither probe an internal unit-type representation nor localize where dimensional errors originate. (3) Human-science education literature documents pervasive, catastrophic dimensional-analysis errors and the power of dimensional-homogeneity checks (Using Math in Physics: Dimensional Analysis 2021; Check Your Work: Dimensional Homogeneity 2023); we transfer this phenomenon into LLMs and give it a mechanistic account. The central confound we address up front is LEXICAL: a probe could merely read the surface unit token ('mg') rather than an abstract dimension; our design therefore leads with lexical controls (synonyms, non-adjacent unit strings, unit-token ablation, and control prompts with identical tokens but different dimension labels), and if the signal is purely lexical the core novelty is an informative negative result. No prior work asks whether LLMs maintain a consulted internal dimension representation.
Abstract: Human students and even engineers routinely make dimensional errors — adding a length to a time, forgetting a conversion, reporting the wrong unit — and dimensional-consistency checking is a classic remedy. We ask whether reasoning language models share this blind spot and, mechanistically, why. We hypothesize that models linearly encode the physical DIMENSION (unit-type: length, time, mass, concentration, dose-per-mass) of each quantity at specific layers and step boundaries, separately from its magnitude, but frequently fail to consult this representation where a dimensionally-inconsistent operation is committed. We test two independently falsifiable claims — representational existence and a causal consultation gap — on templated unit-conversion and physics/engineering problems and, for high stakes, medication-STYLE dosing scenarios (mg vs mg/kg vs mL) using open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). We first show dimensional errors are a distinct failure class from magnitude/arithmetic errors: models often compute the right number but attach the wrong unit. We then train linear probes to decode unit-type, show it is separable from magnitude AND from the literal unit token via lexical controls (synonyms, non-adjacent tokens), and that it is often correct even on error-committing steps. We localize the representation and test causal involvement via activation patching, then build a training-free dimensional-consistency monitor that flags incompatible operations. Because dimension tracking is a reusable consistency check across science and math, the monitor targets calculator-augmented reasoning and tool-use agents broadly, not only medicine. A negative outcome (purely lexical signal, or genuine not-knowing) is itself informative about where unit reliability breaks down.
Experiments:
All experiments use open reasoning models with frozen weights (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B thinking mode); the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear probes. Generation uses temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Because no public benchmark annotates per-step unit-types, we CONSTRUCT three sets with ground-truth dimension labels by construction and reuse their templates across all experiments: (S1) templated unit-conversion chains (km/h->m/s, nested SI-prefix conversions) — 1500 items generated from ~30 templates; (S2) multi-step physics/engineering word problems with known intermediate dimensions and correct final unit — 1000 items adapted from open physics-problem templates; (S3) medication-dosing scenarios (dose from weight in kg, concentration in mg/mL, dose in mg/kg, with g<->mg and mL<->L conversion traps) — 800 items from ~20 clinician-reviewed templates. Steps are segmented by native delimiters. 'Current working quantity' and its true unit-type are known from the template generator, removing annotation ambiguity.

Experiment 1 (H2 — dimensional-error phenomenon distinct from magnitude): Tests that models commit dimensional errors that are separate from arithmetic errors, i.e. often the right number with the wrong unit. Data: S1(1500), S2(1000), S3(800), 3 generations each. Each error is classified DIMENSIONAL (wrong unit-type / incompatible combination / missing conversion / wrong final unit) vs MAGNITUDE (right units, wrong number) by template-based parsing plus an LLM-judge, with human spot-checks on 300 items (report Cohen's kappa; parsing is primary if kappa>=0.7). Systems compared: the four models across the three sets. Decisive metric FIRST: the fraction of all errors that are dimensional AND numerically-correct ('right number, wrong unit'). Convincing result: this fraction is >= 15% of errors in >=3 of 4 models on >=2 of 3 sets, establishing dimensional errors as a non-trivial, distinct failure class. Indecision band: 5-15% — present but marginal, reported as a minor failure mode weakening the paper's premise. Negative result (< 5%, i.e. nearly all errors are arithmetic): there is no separate dimensional blind spot; the central premise fails and the mechanistic experiments are not pursued. We report dosing (S3) separately for its safety stakes.

Experiment 2 (H1 — dimension encoded separately from magnitude): Tests that a linear direction decodes the unit-type of the current working quantity, distinct from its magnitude. Data: step-boundary activations from Experiment-1 traces, labeled by true unit-type (classes: length/time/mass/volume/concentration/dose-per-mass/dimensionless/other); item-level 70/15/15 split; probe = multinomial logistic regression, L2, one per layer, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the unit-type probe versus a reproduced log-magnitude regressor on the same activations; and critical controls that isolate the dimension code from confounds — a lexical control (probe trained where the unit STRING 'mg' is not token-adjacent, tested across notations/synonyms mg vs milligram), plus magnitude-only, unit-token-only, and task-format-only predictor baselines trained on the same activations; probe layer/step are selected on the validation split (never the test split) to avoid circularity. Decisive metric FIRST: unit-type classification accuracy (macro-F1) on held-out items, and the principal angle between the unit-type subspace and the magnitude direction. Convincing result: macro-F1 >= 0.70 (well above the majority-class baseline reported alongside), principal angle >= 30 degrees (not collinear with magnitude), and F1 drops by < 0.10 under the cross-notation lexical control. Indecision band: F1 0.55-0.70, or angle 15-30 degrees, or a lexical-control drop of 0.10-0.25 — dimension is encoded but weakly or partly lexically, reported as such. Negative result (F1 near majority baseline, or angle < 15 degrees, or F1 collapses under the lexical control): there is no abstract dimension representation separate from magnitude/token identity; H1 fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — know-but-dont-check gap): Tests that on steps where the model commits a dimensional error, the internal unit-types of the input operands are nonetheless often correct. Data: from Experiment-1, the subset of steps flagged as dimensional errors (target >= 500 such steps aggregated across models/sets; if fewer, we report power limits) plus a matched set of correct steps. Read the Experiment-2 unit-type probe on the input operands just before the erroneous operation. Decisive metric FIRST: probe accuracy on the operands of error-committing steps (the internal unit-type is correct even though the executed operation is invalid). Convincing result: operand unit-type probe accuracy on error steps >= 0.60 and within 0.15 of its accuracy on correct steps — i.e. the information was available but unused, quantifying the gap. Indecision band: error-step probe accuracy 0.45-0.60 — the model may partly not know the units, blurring know-vs-dont-check; reported as ambiguous. Negative result (probe accuracy near chance on error steps): the model does NOT internally know the correct units when it errs, so this is a capability gap, not a consultation gap; H2's 'know-but-dont-check' framing fails (though the phenomenon and probe stand).

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal reality of the dimension representation): Tests that the unit-type representation causally controls whether the model commits the dimensional error. Data: 400 about-to-err steps identified in Experiment 3. Intervention: activation-patch the correct unit-type representation (from a matched correct-unit context) into the localized components at the erring step; frozen weights; dose-response over patch strength. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) correct-unit patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target control on unrelated correct items. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in dimensional-error rate at the patched step under the correct-unit patch versus controls. Convincing result: correct-unit patch cuts the dimensional-error rate by >= 10 absolute points with CI excluding 0, a monotone dose-response, no comparable effect from the random-direction patch, and off-target accuracy preserved within 1 point. Indecision band: 3-10 points, or random-direction patch reproducing >=50% of the effect — causality not cleanly shown. Negative result (no reduction, or non-specific): the representation is not causal for the error; H3 fails.

Experiment 5 (H5 — training-free dimensional-consistency monitor): Tests that a monitor reading the internal unit-type catches unit errors the model misses, more cheaply than prompting or post-hoc checking. Data: full S1/S2/S3, 3 seeds. Monitor: at each step boundary, read the Experiment-2 probe on the operands; flag when an operation combines incompatible dimensions or the running dimension diverges from the target answer's dimension, optionally triggering a unit-check re-derivation. Systems compared: (a) no monitor, (b) 'check your units' self-verification prompt, (c) the repurposed arithmetic-error probe from prior work, (d) an LLM-judge post-hoc checker, (e) our internal-representation monitor. Decisive metric FIRST: dimensional-error catch rate (recall of true dimensional errors) at matched false-flag rate on correct traces, plus corrected-answer rate after re-derivation and added tokens. Convincing result: the internal monitor achieves >= 15 points higher recall than the best baseline at equal false-flag rate (<= 5%), while adding fewer tokens than the post-hoc LLM checker. Indecision band: recall advantage 5-15 points, or false-flag rate 5-10% — useful but not decisively better, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no recall advantage, or false-flag rate > 10%): the internal representation gives no practical monitoring benefit; H5 fails though H1-H3 remain.

Experiment 6 (H4 — safety-critical dosing focus): Tests that the phenomenon and the monitor matter most in medication dosing. Data: S3 (800), with the subset of scenarios whose traps yield order-of-magnitude (10x) dosing errors from g/mg or mL/L confusion isolated. Decisive metric FIRST: catch rate of 10x dosing errors by the internal monitor versus baselines, and the residual dangerous-error rate after the monitor. Convincing result: the monitor catches >= 80% of 10x dosing errors at <= 5% false-flag, cutting residual dangerous errors by >= half relative to no monitor. Indecision band: catch rate 50-80% — meaningful but insufficient for the safety framing, reported with the residual failure modes catalogued. Negative result (< 50% caught): the monitor does not deliver the safety benefit the hypothesis claims for dosing; H4's practical claim fails. These are synthetic scenarios and are not clinical validation.

Experiment 7 (H1/H2 generalization and scale): Tests whether the probe and monitor transfer without retraining and whether the know-but-dont-check gap shrinks with scale. Data: probe/monitor fit on one set+model, applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-set unit-type F1 and cross-set monitor recall under transfer, and the trend of the Experiment-3 gap (encode-well-but-consult-poorly) across model scale. Convincing result: transferred F1 within 0.10 of in-domain, transferred recall >= half the in-domain value, and a monotone shrink of the consultation gap from 1.5B to 14B. Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or a non-monotone but downward scale trend — partial generalization, reported as scale/family-specific. Negative result (no transfer, flat scale trend): the representation and gap are idiosyncratic per model/set, reported as a boundary characterization.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Identifying the 'current working quantity' and annotating ground-truth unit-types at each step is nontrivial; we mitigate with templated problems (known dimensions by construction), parsing plus LLM-judge, and human validation with reported agreement. The unit-type representation may be inseparable from magnitude or from surface token identity of the unit string (a probe could just read the literal 'mg' token rather than an abstract dimension); we control by testing generalization across notations/synonyms (mg vs milligram), across problems where the unit token is not adjacent, and via the separability analysis and causal patching—if the signal is purely lexical that is an informative negative result. Dimensional errors may be rarer in strong models, limiting statistical power (itself a boundary-condition finding on the know-but-dont-check gap vs scale). The patching intervention could push activations off-distribution and introduce new errors; matched-random-direction controls and validity checks are included. The monitor may over-flag on legitimately dimensionless or context-dependent quantities (e.g., ratios), inflating false positives; we tune thresholds and report precision. Medication-dosing scenarios are synthetic and should not be treated as clinical validation—they demonstrate the failure mode, not a deployable clinical tool. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and reasoning-step segmentation requires clear delimiters.
